claims.text: On 17 December 2010 the owner gave the keynote at IBWAS'10, OWASP's Ibero-American web application security conference, at ISCTE in Lisbon.
claims.quote: On 17 December 2010 I gave the keynote at IBWAS'10, OWASP's Ibero-American web application security conference, at ISCTE in Lisbon.

claims.text: The keynote had 168 slides, five proposed focuses and twelve proposed actions.
claims.quote: The IBWAS keynote: 168 slides, five focuses, twelve actions.

claims.text: A few weeks later the owner wrote that there were thought-provoking ideas in the talk and he did not expect some to become reality any time soon; the press picked up the line that Portugal could be the Switzerland of hacking.
claims.quote: I don't expect that some of them will become reality any time soon

claims.text: The five focuses were: treat software and application security with the respect it deserves; view it as business intelligence; as competitive advantage; make the application security market work; and use OWASP as a resource and enabler.
claims.quote: make the application security market "work"; and use OWASP as a resource and enabler

claims.text: Application security as business intelligence, understanding how your software really works, is exactly what the owner argues today for agents and graphs.
claims.quote: Today that is exactly what I argue for agents and graphs: the value of GenAI is that it can understand

claims.text: The fourth focus, a market that works, is still the weakest: buyers still cannot easily tell secure software from insecure software.
claims.quote: buyers still cannot easily tell secure software from insecure software

claims.text: The twelve actions for government or industry included allowing ethical hacking, security score cards, procurement requirements, liability, a vulnerability-disclosure agency, rewriting computer laws, paying for open-source security, insurance, holding fewer assets, better journalism and proper SSL for half of websites.
claims.quote: allow ethical hacking; publish the results of security reviews as score cards; put security requirements in procurement

claims.text: From 9 December 2026 the EU's Product Liability Directive brings software, standalone or embedded, under strict no-fault liability; the slide asked for government and listed companies, and the law went further.
claims.quote: brings software, standalone or embedded, under strict, no-fault liability

claims.text: Europe has its own vulnerability database, run by ENISA since May 2025, and since 11 September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours.
claims.quote: requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours

claims.text: Portugal's new cybersecurity law, Decreto-Lei 125/2025, which transposes NIS2, came into force on 3 April 2026 with the national cybersecurity centre as its authority.
claims.quote: came into force on 3 April 2026, with the national cybersecurity centre as its authority

claims.text: Proper SSL was achieved and more: Google's transparency report shows most pages loaded in Chrome now use HTTPS, far past the 50% of websites the slide asked for.
claims.quote: shows most pages loaded in Chrome now use HTTPS, far past my 50%

value.unit: percent of websites with proper SSL, the 2010 target

claims.text: What did not come true: score cards for software, an insurance market that prices application security well, and paying for open-source security at the scale it needs.
claims.quote: Score cards for software, an insurance market that prices application security well, and paying for open-source security at the scale it needs.

claims.text: Reducing the assets held is the action the owner would put first today: the best way to protect data is not to have it, or to hold only ciphertext, which is what sgit does.
claims.quote: the best way to protect data is not to have it, or to hold only ciphertext

claims.text: The middle of the deck compared software to health and safety: a minimum level of quality is expected from water, food, cars and planes, with laws to regulate them, and very little in software.
claims.quote: we expect a minimum level of quality from water, food, cars and planes, and have laws that regulate them

claims.text: The analogy was right and the mechanism was wrong: fear and a big incident did not move governments quickly; a decade of slow, unglamorous regulation did.
claims.quote: I thought fear, and a big enough incident, would move governments quickly. What moved them was a decade of slow, unglamorous regulation.

claims.text: The challenge to Portugal, a country described as depressed with nothing to lose, was to build an open, ethical security industry; it cost no money and took only courage, focus and commitment.
claims.quote: It only takes courage, focus and commitment

claims.text: The core still stands: a small country can choose a sector and lead in it, the same argument the owner made sixteen years later about AI in Judo for small countries.
claims.quote: a small country can choose a sector and lead in it

claims.text: Portugal is no longer the depressed country of 2010, but it did not become the Switzerland of hacking; that thread is picked up by the 2016 and 2024 talks.
claims.quote: But Portugal did not become the Switzerland of hacking.

claims.text: Not that the talk caused any of it: the EU's laws have their own long history.
claims.quote: The EU's laws have their own long history.

claims.text: The commentary is the owner's, now; the slides are from 2010, unchanged.
claims.quote: The slides are from 2010, unchanged.

claims.text: The video seems to be gone; the slides are the record.
claims.quote: The video seems to be gone. The slides are the record.

claims.text: This is the first of a series of articles on the owner's talks about Portugal, ahead of a new edition of Hacking Portugal.
claims.quote: This is the first of a series of articles on the talks I have given about Portugal, ahead of a new edition of Hacking Portugal.
